card vi-sysdiag-render  [decided]
The agent places. A program does the pixel arithmetic and checks it
why: #vi-sysdiag-svg read well because the agent chose the lanes and the order, not because the SVG was hand-tuned. The hand-tuning is the cost: in .werk/diagram-a.svg the agent computed 22 label plates as chars * 5.6 + 8 and 22 box borders by hand. That arithmetic is mechanical, it is where the spacing errors came from, and a program does it exactly.
subtree: 26 cards, 8 open, 5 proto, 13 decided, 4 unchallenged, 2 stale

Split the drawing in two, along the line the prototype already drew.

**Intent (the agent writes it).** Which lane a node sits in, which order inside the lane, which nodes group, which of the seven edge colours an edge carries, and the label text. This is judgement. Mermaid failed at exactly this, because its auto-layout took the choice away — see #vi-sysdiag-svg.

**Arithmetic (a program does it).** Text measurement, box size from text, label plate size and centring, lane box size from its contents, the point where an arrow meets a border, grid spacing, and the viewBox. None of this needs judgement. All of it was done by hand in `.werk/diagram-a.svg`, 44 times.

The program is a resolver over a grid, not a layout engine. It never chooses which node goes where. Given lane + index it computes x and y. That is the difference from #vi-sysdiag-format:opt0, which was rejected as "layout code" when the assumption was still that some program must decide positions.

Text measurement has an exact answer here: werk renders its own picture in a browser, so the renderer runs client-side and calls `measureText`. No font metrics table, no `chars * 5.6` estimate.

card vi-sysdiag-grid  [proto]
Grid resolver: the agent draws the diagram on a topological grid, a tile grammar checks it, a program renders it
why: #vi-sysdiag-intent only lets the agent control which cards sit in which row. Edges, labels and spacing are left to the resolver, and six rounds of fixes on #vi-sysdiag-render-polish show the agent cannot see what it produced without rendering and screenshotting. A grid the agent writes cell by cell is legible to its own author before anything is rendered.
subtree: 14 cards, 2 open, 5 proto, 7 decided, 1 unchallenged, 2 stale

Eryks design, three parts: reuse Mermaid syntax for relations, card content and ids; add a grid DSL for placement, constrained by formal adjacency rules; render the checked grid with a deterministic program and parametrised components.

This is the same Substance/Style split as #penrose - Mermaid says what exists, the grid says where it goes - applied to a medium the author can read back.

**The reason this is worth building, stated plainly.** Not control. Legibility. Every defect this session was found by Eryk looking at a picture, never by me reading the input. An intent file cannot be proofread. A grid can: it is a low-fidelity rendering of itself. That closes the loop #vi-sysdiag-lint only half closed - the checker catches what it has a rule for, the grid shows everything else.

**Prior art, none of it invented here.** #tiling-systems is the formal name for rules 1.1 to 1.7. #wang-wfc is the same constraint structure solved generatively. #kandinsky is exactly boxes-on-coarse-grid, edges-on-fine-grid, and warns that optimising it is NP-complete. #svgbob is a working text-grid-to-SVG renderer. #css-grid-areas is the DSL, already shipped, with the rectangle rule and the same-token-count rule worth copying verbatim.

**Three decisions that have to be made before any code.** See the notes on this card.

  -> refines         vi-sysdiag-render  The agent places. A program does the pixel arithmetic and checks it
  -> supported_by    tiling-systems  Tiling systems / recognizable picture languages: the formal name for a 2D language defined by allowed tiles
  -> supported_by    wang-wfc  Wang tiles and Wave Function Collapse: the same constraints, run generatively instead of as a check
  -> supported_by    kandinsky  The Kandinsky model: boxes on a coarse grid, edges routed on a finer grid
  -> supported_by    svgbob  svgbob, ditaa, a2s: working implementations of text grid in, styled SVG out
  -> supported_by    css-grid-areas  CSS grid-template-areas: the mainstream DSL that is already ASCII-art placement with a validity rule
  -> supported_by    penrose  Penrose: Substance says what exists, Style says how it looks, and Substance holds no numbers
  -> depends_on      vi-sysdiag-render  The agent places. A program does the pixel arithmetic and checks it
  -> alternative_to  vi-sysdiag-intent  The intent file: nested groups, rows, and edges with a colour class. Eight keywords
  <- refines         vi-sysdiag-grid-mvp  Step 1 is not code: hand-author one grid for six cards and see if it reads  (9 cards, 2 open, 1 proto, 6 decided, 1 unchallenged, 1 stale)

card vi-sysdiag-grid-scale  [decided]
Built the full 21-card diagram — 2 real rendering bugs found and fixed, 1 new gap found
why: Translated .werk/diagram.mmd (21 cards, 22 edges) into .werk/diagram-grid-full.wgrid/.svg, wired to the app as 'Grid (full)'. Findings, in order of consequence:

1. FIXED — check.ts wrongly flagged a valid 1-cell path (two cards stacked with exactly one gap row between them) as 'isolated', because its degree math only recognises OTHER path cells as neighbours. A cell touching both from and to directly has degree 0 and was rejected outright. Never triggered before because every edge in the 4-card prototype happened to span 3+ cells.

2. FIXED, more serious — the same 1-cell case broke resolve.ts's rendering even where the checker allowed it: clipping the single point to the 'to' card overwrote the earlier clip to the 'from' card at the same array index, collapsing the line to one point. 20 of this diagram's 22 edges rendered as invisible before the fix (confirmed by grep on the SVG's path d= attributes, not by eye). A subagent's visual QA pass on the broken render reported 'no floating ends found' — flatly wrong, caught only by checking the SVG source directly. Fixed the same way bridgedPathPoints already handled its own 1-cell arms: duplicate the point, clip each copy to a different card.

3. NOT FIXED, new gap — a group's frame is the bounding box of its members (#vi-sysdiag-grid-gaps item 2 already flagged this is metric, not reserved space). At this scale it has a second failure mode: STORE's three members (log, chatlog, allow) sit far apart, so STORE's frame rectangle geometrically swallows three unrelated cards (issue tracker, permission gate, claude code child) that are not its members. Verified by reading the actual computed rect coordinates, not by looking at the picture.

4. Authoring cost does not scale by hand. Two edges crossing group boundaries (gate_approvebar, a back edge; cli_log) needed a dedicated side corridor column and a bottom-margin detour row, worked out by manual adjacency tracing. The grid text itself (19 rows x 37 cols) was only tractable to produce with a throwaway script turning a hand-designed cell list into padded rows — typing it directly was not realistic. The checker and renderer held up fine at 21 cards once (1) and (2) were fixed; the authoring step is what does not scale.

Scope cuts, not findings: edge labels skipped entirely (structure-only, to keep this bounded); 3 dotted Mermaid edges became solid (no dashed-stroke support); dev->proc (an edge into a subgraph, not a card) retargeted to dev->runner since R3 requires touching a card.
  -> refines         vi-sysdiag-grid-gaps  Five things the grid format cannot express yet, found by building it once
  -> depends_on      vi-sysdiag-grid  Grid resolver: the agent draws the diagram on a topological grid, a tile grammar checks it, a program renders it
  <- depends_on      vi-sysdiag-grid-singlecell-scale  At 21-card scale, single-cell is not a size change — it breaks the grid
  <- depends_on      vi-sysdiag-grid-minimal  From-scratch minimal-cell full grid: 12x22, down from 39x23

# #vi-sysdiag-grid at scale — the real 21-card architecture (see .werk/diagram.mmd for the
# source Mermaid this was translated from), not the 4-card mv/cp/st/lv prototype.
#
# Two known losses in the translation, both worth recording on #vi-sysdiag-grid-gaps:
#   - Mermaid's three dotted edges (child->gate, gate->approvebar, log->tracker) become solid
#     here. The grid pipeline has no dashed-stroke option yet.
#   - `dev -->|reloads the server| proc` targeted a SUBGRAPH, not a card. A grid edge must
#     touch a card (R3), so it is retargeted to `runner` here.
#
# Third variant, from scratch, per #vi-sysdiag-grid-singlecell-scale: diagram-grid-full.wgrid
# gave every card 2 rows (bookkeeping only) and 3+ columns (padding around 1 real touch
# column). diagram-grid-full-flat.wgrid proved the 2nd row was dead weight. diagram-grid-
# full-flat-narrow.wgrid then deleted only the padding columns no edge anywhere ever touched
# — 8 of 39. That mechanical approach was exhausted: most of the remaining width came from the
# 2 long detour lanes (gate_approvebar, cli_log) eating columns other cards would otherwise
# give up, not from any card's own need.
#
# This file is authored from scratch instead: every card starts at 1 row x 1 column, and is
# widened only when it has more than 1 edge attaching from the SAME single direction (a single
# cell already has all 4 neighbours at once, so edges on different faces never force width).
# Counting from the edge list above:
#   - state:  4 columns — 4 edges arrive from the north (tree, graph3d, detail, rollup); its
#     own south edge (to foldfn) reuses one of those 4 columns.
#   - live:   5 columns — 5 edges arrive from the north (approvebar, composer, transcript,
#     tabs, header); its own south edge (to runner) reuses one of those 5.
#   - runner: 3 columns — 3 edges leave south (to chatlog, lock, child); its north edge (from
#     live) and east edge (from dev) each reuse one of those 3 columns.
#   - child:  2 columns — 2 edges leave south (to gate, to cli), placed contiguously; its own
#     north edge (from runner) reuses one of the 2.
# Every other card, including gate and cli, stayed 1x1: gate receives child_gate from the
# north and gate_allow leaves south (1 each), and gate_approvebar is routed to touch gate's
# WEST face instead of north — a different face, so it adds no width. Symmetrically cli
# receives child_cli from the north, and cli_log is routed to touch cli's EAST face instead —
# again a different face. Both of gate/cli would have needed 2 columns had the detour lanes
# reused the same face as the existing fan-in edge; routing them to a free face instead is
# what keeps gate and cli at 1x1. (This corrects the task's own working guess that gate would
# need width — a smarter face assignment for the detour avoids it.)
#
# The 2 detours run in their own dedicated lane, never sharing a column with a card's own
# span:
#   - gate_approvebar: a single column (separate from every card's columns) running the full
#     height from approvebar's row down to gate's row, then a short 2-cell horizontal jog at
#     gate's own row to reach gate's west face.
#   - cli_log: a column just east of log, running down to the bottom row, a horizontal jog
#     along that otherwise-empty bottom row, then a second column just east of cli, running
#     back up to touch cli's east face. This is a genuine U-shape (down, across, back up), so
#     it still trips the same "U-shaped detour" warning the wider versions did — narrower
#     authored cells, not a straighter line.
#
# Every edge in the content section carries a label, and R4 requires a label to split its
# path into two pieces it bridges (never sit beside an unbroken path) — so every hop between
# two directly-connected card rows still costs the same 3 gap rows (path, label, path) as the
# earlier variants. Row count is therefore close to unchanged; only column width shrank.
#
# Added `diagram`, in MAP VIEW alongside tree/graph3d/

`paintOrder` is a topological sort over one relation — a hopping edge lands after every edge it hops — seeded in document order, so an edge that hops nothing keeps the place the author gave it. A cycle (A hops B at one crossing, B hops A at another) has no paint order that works: those edges keep document order and the build warns, rather than drawing one crossing the wrong way round in silence.
